patterns.signal: The request contains fuzzy words like 'duplicate', 'clean up' or 'fast' that two people could read differently
patterns.why: Pin down inputs, outputs, out-of-scope behaviour and edge cases before any steps. Ten minutes of definition prevents code that runs and solves the wrong problem.

patterns.signal: A feature request names a solution ('remove duplicate customers') but not the outcome anyone actually wants
patterns.use: Ask for the goal behind the request
patterns.why: The real need (cleaner mailing lists? correct billing?) changes scope and edge cases. Skip it only when the goal is already obvious and agreed.

patterns.signal: Raw input goes through several transformations before it becomes the output you need
patterns.why: Each stage gets a small contract you can test and replace alone, e.g. `walk_files` then `group_by` then `content_hash`. Splitting by tech layer ('the DB part') hides the real problem.

patterns.signal: An expensive check (hashing, network call, full compare) would run on every item, but most items can be ruled out cheaply
patterns.why: Grouping by file size before hashing only hashes files whose sizes collide. The cheap key must be a necessary condition, or you will drop true matches.

patterns.signal: A sub-problem smells familiar: grouping by key, ordering, shortest route, matching brackets, parsing text
patterns.why: Recognising sorting, grouping, graph search or parsing gives you a proven algorithm and its known edge cases. Check the fit: a near-match with different constraints can mislead.

patterns.signal: You cannot convince yourself a loop is correct without tracing many inputs by hand
patterns.why: Write the fact that holds before and after every iteration, e.g. 'target, if present, is in `items[lo..hi]`'. Correctness then follows from preserving it at each step.

patterns.signal: A loop like binary search hangs on some inputs even though every update looks logically safe
patterns.why: An invariant can stay true while the range stops shrinking, as with `lo = mid`. Name a quantity that strictly decreases each iteration, such as `hi - lo`.

patterns.signal: You describe one piece of the design and the sentence needs 'and' to cover what it does
patterns.why: A piece with one job has one contract and one reason to change. Stop splitting when pieces become so small that wiring them costs more than it clarifies.

patterns.signal: A sub-problem can only be verified by running the whole system end to end
patterns.why: If a piece needs everything else to check it, the cut is in the wrong place. Move the boundary so the piece takes plain data in and returns plain data out.

patterns.signal: The design covers the happy path, and nobody has said what happens with empty, single, huge or malformed input
patterns.why: Most real defects live at these edges. Listing them during design shapes the contract; discovering them in production means rework and data cleanup.

patterns.signal: The problem is large and you cannot see where to start or how the parts will fit together
patterns.why: Build the simplest version that goes from real input to real output, then deepen each stage. It surfaces integration problems early, at the cost of temporarily crude stages.

patterns.signal: A bare number like `price = 1999` travels through the code and nobody can say its unit or currency without reading the source
patterns.why: A small type carries meaning and rejects nonsense like adding dollars to euros. Costs a little ceremony; skip it for purely local, short-lived values.

patterns.signal: Fields can disagree with each other, e.g. `isLoggedIn == false` while `email` is set
patterns.why: Model distinct states as distinct types (Anonymous or LoggedIn) so the contradiction cannot be built. Removes defensive checks everywhere, but changing states needs more types.

patterns.signal: A function signature takes two or three booleans and call sites read like `render(true, false, true)`
patterns.use: Replace flag arguments with a type
patterns.why: Booleans usually hide a missing concept: an enum, an options object or separate functions. Call sites become self-explaining and impossible combinations become visible.

patterns.signal: The data supports the feature, but every common operation needs a scan or awkward conversion
patterns.why: A list, a map from date to events and an interval tree describe the same calendar but make different queries cheap. Pick for the frequent queries, not for the first one written.

patterns.signal: Logic calls `new Date()`, randomness or the network directly, so tests are slow, flaky or impossible
patterns.use: Inject a seam (fake clock, fake gateway)
patterns.why: Depend on a narrow `Clock` interface and pass a `FakeClock` in tests. Adds one parameter or constructor argument; do not add seams where no test or swap needs them.

patterns.signal: You expect to swap a backend (in-memory dict now, Redis later) and callers are spread across the codebase
patterns.use: Depend on the interface, not the implementation
patterns.why: If callers only use `get` and `put`, the swap touches one class. State failure behaviour (miss, timeout) in the contract or the new backend will surprise callers.

patterns.signal: A class exposes a getter and setter for every field and callers still do all the real work
patterns.use: Deep module: small interface, rich behaviour
patterns.why: An abstraction earns its keep by hiding complexity per concept learned, like `sort`. A wide interface mirroring internals hides nothing and freezes the implementation.

patterns.signal: After one use case, someone proposes a generic plugin framework 'for flexibility'
patterns.use: Rule of three (wait for real variation)
patterns.why: With about three real examples you can see what actually varies. Building early guesses the axis of change and usually guesses wrong; only one-way-door APIs justify earlier design.

patterns.signal: A shared helper keeps gaining boolean parameters and `if` branches, one per caller
patterns.use: Inline the wrong abstraction, then re-extract
patterns.why: Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction. Copy the code back into callers, delete unused branches, and extract again once the real common part is clear.

patterns.signal: An ORM page is slow; logs show one query per row when looping and touching `order.customer`
patterns.use: Learn one layer down (fix the N+1 query)
patterns.why: The object abstraction leaked: each lazy access is a round trip. Use eager loading or one batched query; it may load more data than needed, so measure.

patterns.signal: A wrapper class just forwards every call to the thing it wraps and renames the methods
patterns.why: Indirection without hiding adds names to learn and code to keep in sync. Keep a wrapper only when it narrows the interface, adapts a mismatch or isolates a vendor.

patterns.signal: Callers wrap a function in try/except or null checks because nobody knows what it does when things fail
patterns.use: Put failure modes in the contract
patterns.why: Document or type what happens on missing data, timeout or bad input (return value, error type, retry). Callers can then handle failure once, correctly, instead of guessing.

patterns.signal: It worked at a known release and fails at HEAD, with many commits in between
patterns.why: Each test halves the suspect range, so 1,000 commits need about 10 runs. Needs a reliable, scripted repro; `git bisect run` automates it. Flaky tests mislead it.

patterns.signal: A large input file, config or scene triggers the bug, but you cannot tell which part matters
patterns.why: Repeatedly halve the input and keep whichever half still fails. A tiny case leaves few places for the bug to hide and becomes your regression test.

patterns.signal: The bug shows up in about 1 run in 20 and vanishes when you look
patterns.why: Loop the test, fix seeds, vary timing or load until it fails on demand. Intermittency points at concurrency, ordering or environment; one green run proves nothing.

patterns.signal: Bad data enters a long pipeline and comes out wrong, and you do not know which stage corrupts it
patterns.why: Check or assert the value at the midpoint stage, then halve again on the side that is already wrong. Finds the stage in log steps instead of reading every stage.

patterns.signal: A long stack trace mixes framework and library frames with a few of your own
patterns.use: Read the message, then the innermost own frame
patterns.why: The exception type and message say what went wrong; the deepest frame in your code shows where the bad value was used. Library frames are rarely where the defect is.

patterns.signal: A crash on `None` or null happens deep in a calculation, and the obvious patch is a null check right there
patterns.why: Ask how a priceless item reached the cart, not how to survive it. A guard at the crash site hides the defect and lets bad data spread further.

patterns.signal: You suspect a cause ('the cache is stale') and are about to change code to see if the symptom goes away
patterns.use: Predict, then run the falsifying experiment
patterns.why: Say what else must be true if the hypothesis holds (e.g. cache key and timestamp in logs) and run the cheapest test that could prove it wrong. Guess-and-patch leaves the cause.

patterns.signal: You changed several suspicious things at once and the bug went away
patterns.use: Change one variable at a time
patterns.why: With several edits you cannot tell which mattered, and the others may hide a second bug. Revert, then reapply one change per run. Slower per step, far faster overall.

patterns.signal: It works on your machine and fails in CI, staging or on a colleague's setup
patterns.why: List versions, env vars, config, data and OS between the good and bad setups, then bisect the differences. Assumptions about 'identical' environments are often wrong.

patterns.signal: Logs say a step ran correctly, yet the observed behaviour contradicts them
patterns.why: Log lines describe what the author intended and can be stale or misplaced. Inspect the actual value at runtime; trust behaviour over messages.

patterns.signal: You have stared at the same code for an hour and every assumption still seems fine
patterns.use: Rubber duck (explain it step by step)
patterns.why: Stating each assumption in order, aloud or in a written bug report, often exposes the false one mid-sentence. Costs minutes; also makes a ready-made handoff if you need help.

patterns.signal: You found the cause and are about to commit the fix
patterns.why: Write a test that fails before the fix and passes after. It proves you fixed this cause and stops the bug returning; skipping it leaves the fix unverified.

patterns.signal: A proposal ('add a cache', 'go microservices') lists only benefits
patterns.use: Name what each option makes worse
patterns.why: Every option buys something with something else: a cache buys speed with staleness and invalidation work. Ask for 2-3 options with their costs before choosing.

patterns.signal: Someone asks whether a design can handle the load and there are no numbers yet
patterns.why: Users x actions per day / ~100k seconds gives average QPS in minutes. Aim for the right order of magnitude; write units so mistakes show up.

patterns.signal: A capacity plan is sized on the average request rate
patterns.use: Apply a peak factor and watch the tail
patterns.why: Traffic peaks at several times the average and users feel p99, not the mean. Size for peak plus headroom; sizing for the average guarantees overload at busy hours.

patterns.signal: A question about storing photos, logs or events for millions of users
patterns.use: Storage estimate: count x size x copies
patterns.why: 5M users x 2 MB is 10 TB before replication and backups. The number decides between database, object storage and tiering long before any code is written.

patterns.signal: A design puts a database, cache or HTTP call inside a loop over many items
patterns.why: 10,000 calls at 0.5 ms is 5 s; one batched query takes tens of ms. Memory, SSD, datacentre and cross-continent costs differ by orders of magnitude, so count remote calls.

patterns.signal: Per-item overhead dominates a job and total throughput is too low, but each item can wait a little
patterns.why: Amortises fixed cost per call across many items and raises throughput. Increases per-item latency and makes a single failure affect a whole batch.

patterns.signal: Reads are slow because each one recomputes or joins the same data, and reads vastly outnumber writes
patterns.why: Indexes, lookup tables and denormalised copies make reads cheap. You pay in storage, slower writes and keeping copies consistent when the source changes.

patterns.signal: The team debates for days over a choice that sits behind a thin interface and could be swapped later
patterns.why: Cheap-to-undo decisions do not deserve long analysis; pick a reasonable option and learn from use. Analysis paralysis on reversible choices costs more than a wrong pick.

patterns.signal: The choice is a public API shape, a schema with live data, a deletion policy or a long vendor contract
patterns.use: One-way door: slow down and prototype
patterns.why: Hard-to-reverse decisions deserve review, a spike and written alternatives. Applying this rigour to every decision instead would stall the team.

patterns.signal: A risky decision looks one-way, but parts of it could be staged or hidden behind something swappable
patterns.use: Convert a one-way door into a two-way door
patterns.why: Feature flags, adapters, dual writes and versioned APIs make rollback possible. They add temporary complexity that must be removed once the decision settles.

patterns.signal: An optimisation is proposed because something 'feels slow', with no profile or timing data
patterns.use: Estimate to choose, measure to confirm
patterns.why: Estimates pick the design; a profiler or benchmark shows where time actually goes. Optimising unmeasured code often speeds up the part that was never the bottleneck.

patterns.signal: The team weighs writing an in-house component against buying or adopting one
patterns.use: Total cost of ownership (build vs buy)
patterns.why: Building costs initial time plus years of maintenance, on-call and upgrades; buying costs money, control and lock-in. Build only what differentiates your product.

patterns.signal: You are dropped into a large unfamiliar repository and asked to change one behaviour
patterns.why: Learn where entry points, domain logic, storage and tests live before opening functions. Reading every file is impossible; a map tells you which few files matter.

patterns.signal: You do not know where a behaviour starts: no obvious `main`, many modules, framework magic
patterns.use: Find the entry point (route, command, handler)
patterns.why: Every behaviour starts at a route table, CLI command, event handler or scheduled job. Search for the URL, command name or event string and follow from there.

patterns.signal: You are reading files top to bottom and an hour later still cannot explain the feature
patterns.use: Trace one concrete scenario end to end
patterns.why: Follow one piece of data from request to database and back. It reads only the code that matters for your change; check afterwards for other callers and config flags.

patterns.signal: Names and comments are unclear and you are unsure what a function is meant to do
patterns.why: Tests are executable examples of what the authors believed the code does. Missing or thin tests are themselves a finding: add one before changing behaviour.

patterns.signal: A line or check looks pointless and you want to delete it
patterns.why: Use `git blame` and the commit message or linked issue to learn what problem it solved. Delete once you know the reason no longer applies, not before.

patterns.signal: You need to know when a symbol, constant or behaviour was introduced or last changed
patterns.why: `git log -S'refund_amount'` lists commits that added or removed the string, with their messages. Far faster than reading diffs, but renamed symbols need a second search.

patterns.signal: A docstring says 'never returns null' but a test or run shows it returning null
patterns.why: Code behaviour is ground truth; comments and names express intent and go stale. Either the code has a bug or the docs are wrong, and both deserve a fix or an issue.

patterns.signal: You (or an agent) concluded a function has only one caller after a plain text search
patterns.use: Check dynamic references before trusting it
patterns.why: Reflection, string-based lookups, DI containers, serialisation, event wiring and engine callbacks (e.g. message-based methods) escape plain search. Run the code or check config to confirm.

patterns.signal: You think you understand a module but cannot say what a specific change will do
patterns.why: Turn the mental model into a testable claim and check it by running the code. A failed prediction is cheap here and expensive after you ship the change.

patterns.signal: Control flow is buried under interfaces, callbacks and indirection, and static reading keeps losing the thread
patterns.use: Step through it in a debugger
patterns.why: Running one request under a debugger shows the real call path and actual values, including overrides and dynamic dispatch. Use it to confirm a path, not to read a whole system.

patterns.signal: You are about to ask a teammate or agent 'how does billing work?'
patterns.why: A question that states the goal, what you read or tried, what you expected and what happened gets a precise answer. Vague questions get vague tours.

patterns.signal: You just spent hours working out what a module does and the docs do not say it
patterns.why: Write the summary you wish you had been given and put it next to the code. It is the cheapest onboarding there is, and must be updated when behaviour changes.
